subject: ophthalmology
title: Retinal detachment and retinal degenerations

steps.tx: A full thickness retinal break lets liquefied vitreous pass under the neurosensory retina and peel it from the pigment epithelium, with flashes, new floaters, dark tobacco dust and a spreading curtain. Nearsightedness, lattice degeneration, trauma and recent cataract surgery all raise the risk. When the **macula** is still attached, surgery proceeds emergently, while a detached macula is repaired within days. Flat tears receive **barrage laser**, wide breaks receive **scleral buckling**, complex disease receives vitrectomy with gas or oil tamponade, and one superior break may suit pneumatic retinopexy.
steps.say: A curtain or shadow that spreads after flashes and new floaters means the retina has detached through a break. When central vision is still preserved, the macula is attached and surgery must happen emergently. Small flat tears can be sealed with laser, while detached retina needs buckling or vitrectomy with gas or oil. The fellow eye also needs careful examination because it carries the same risk.

vis.caption: B-scan ultrasonography shows a detached retinal membrane in the vitreous cavity, with the macula labelled as attached or detached. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: In **tractional detachment**, fibrovascular membranes in proliferative diabetic disease, sickle cell sea fans or retinopathy of prematurity pull the retina into a tented concave shape, and vitrectomy with membrane peeling is needed before the macula is threatened. In **exudative detachment**, fluid from Harada disease, posterior scleritis, tumours or severe hypertension collects under the retina without any break and shifts with posture, so treatment controls the systemic cause. **B scan ultrasound** separates break related detachment from tractional or exudative patterns when haze blocks the view.
steps.say: A tented and immobile retina that is pulled by membranes points to tractional detachment, which needs membrane peeling by vitrectomy. Shifting fluid under the retina without any break points to exudative detachment, which settles when the systemic disease is treated. When blood or haze blocks the view, ultrasound separates these patterns reliably. Combined disease with both traction and breaks needs vitrectomy with tamponade.

steps.tx: This ocular **B scan** shows a bright wavy retinal membrane tethered at the optic nerve head with dark **subretinal fluid** beneath it, which is the classic appearance of detachment when the fundus cannot be seen. The membrane stays anchored at the disc while the rest floats, and its concave tented shape favors tractional disease over a freely mobile break. Recognising this pattern matters because it directs the patient toward vitrectomy with **membrane peeling** rather than laser alone.
steps.say: This ultrasound shows a bright wavy membrane that remains attached at the optic nerve head while fluid collects beneath it. The tethered and concave shape tells you the retina is detached, even when blood or cataract hides the fundus. A membrane pulled by traction looks tented and thick, while exudative fluid shifts freely without a break. Spotting disc attachment with subretinal fluid should make you plan vitrectomy in the exam.

vis.alt: Grayscale ocular ultrasound B scan showing bright wavy tethered retinal membrane attached at optic nerve head with subretinal fluid.
vis.caption: Ocular B scan showing tethered retinal membrane and subretinal fluid Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Retinitis pigmentosa** is a rod cone dystrophy, often autosomal recessive and sometimes part of Usher syndrome with deafness, that causes night blindness first, then bone spicules, narrowed arterioles, waxy disc pallor and tunnel fields with a flat electroretinogram. Vitamin A palmitate may slow decline, gene therapy for RPE65 helps some children, and low vision aids sustain function. **Lattice degeneration** with atrophic holes in nearsighted eyes receives prophylactic laser. **Retinoschisis** splits retinal layers, classically X linked boys with a spoke wheel macula, and is observed unless detachment develops.
steps.say: A young patient with night blindness, bone spicule pigmentation and tunnel vision has retinitis pigmentosa. Narrowed arterioles with a waxy pale disc and a flat electroretinogram confirm the diagnosis. Thin lattice with holes in a nearsighted eye deserves prophylactic laser before a tear forms. A spoke wheel macula in a boy suggests retinoschisis, which is observed unless detachment occurs.

vis.caption: A silicone exoplant indents the sclera beneath the retinal break during scleral buckling, with cryopexy applied and subretinal fluid drained. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Retinopathy of prematurity** follows arrested retinal vascularisation in low birthweight infants given oxygen, progressing through stages to a fibrous ridge with **plus disease**, meaning dilated tortuous posterior vessels, and onward to tractional detachment and blindness. Screening covers infants born very preterm or with very low birth weight, and timely peripheral laser ablation, with anti vascular endothelial growth factor therapy in selected eyes, halts progression. Advanced stages need vitrectomy or buckling. **Aggressive posterior disease** can skip stages rapidly, so oxygen is titrated carefully with neonatal collaboration.
steps.say: A preterm infant on oxygen can develop a ridge with dilated tortuous vessels, which is plus disease in retinopathy of prematurity. Screening of tiny babies catches the ridge before traction detaches the retina. Timely laser to the avascular periphery prevents progression in most eyes. Advanced traction needs vitrectomy, and careful oxygen titration with the neonatal team prevents severe disease.
